posts.text: I was pleased to be quoted by Taylor in this Digital IT News piece, but the more interesting part for me was reading everyone else’s answers. The article asks about the “best use” of enterprise AI. Read all of the responses together and a different question starts to emerge: What has to be true before enterprise AI can be trusted to matter? My answer is context. Enterprises already have extraordinary amounts of intelligence. But we have spent years breaking that intelligence apart. The conversation becomes a recording. The recording becomes a transcript. The transcript becomes a summary. The summary becomes a CRM note. Someone sends an email. Someone creates a task. Someone approves an exception. Then six months later, a human or AI agent is expected to understand why a decision was made. That is not primarily a model problem. It is a records problem. If AI gets the summary but loses the source, the evidence, the sequence, the promises, the qualifications, and what happened next, we should not be surprised when it confidently misunderstands the situation. This is why I keep coming back to the same conviction: AI needs better records. And as agents begin making more consequential decisions, context with provenance will matter a lot more than context alone.

posts.text: When we build multi-agent systems, we divide work into roles. One agent researches, another analyzes, another checks the result. We define their tools and how they exchange information, then expect to replace or upgrade each component without redesigning the whole system. Adding persistent memory complicates that assumption. Agents can retain procedures and lessons from earlier tasks, including expectations about how their teammates behave. Over time, some of what makes an agent effective may depend on the particular team it has worked with. An interesting paper I came across, “Testing Interchangeability in LLM Agent Teams,” investigates this through a controlled swap experiment. The researchers formed eight independent teams per setting. Agents shared the same base model and role prompts, but kept private notebooks across ten episodes together. They then swapped equally experienced agents with matching roles between teams and evaluated the new pairings on held-out tasks. A control announced a replacement but returned the original agent. Task scores changed little, but communication per unit of progress increased by 16–63%. In Hanabi, an experienced agent from another team required more signalling effort than an inexperienced replacement. Longer shared histories increased the swap penalty in the tested conditions. The notebooks contained expectations about who acts without being asked, who needs explicit instructions, what signals mean and when handoffs happen. These habits were stored in text; model weights stayed unchanged. Consider an illustrative research-and-analysis workflow. The researcher learns that its partner checks missing citations automatically, so it stops explicitly flagging them. The analyst learns that an empty field means “still being investigated,” rather than “nothing found.” An equally capable replacement may interpret those signals differently. The tools still connect and the messages still arrive, but the assumptions behind them no longer match. Additional clarification and corrections may preserve the final result while making the workflow more expensive. For builders, the distinction is between knowing how to perform a role and knowing how to perform it with a particular partner. Matching the model, instructions and tools may preserve the first without preserving the second. I would therefore test replacements after a team has accumulated experience, measuring communication and execution cost alongside completion. Evaluating each agent independently, or testing only fresh teams, could miss dependencies that emerge through memory. A design implication worth testing is to separate reusable task knowledge from partner-specific expectations. A procedure for validating a record should transfer between teams. An assumption that another agent always performs that validation needs checking when membership changes. Paper: https://lnkd.in/ejWVnGhT

posts.text: Instinct is the AI agent that has gone viral this month. It is agentic AI in its purest form: an agent that carries out everyday tasks on its own, not one that just answers questions. What we know: → It uses your existing apps and accounts. No new interface to learn. Instinct is trained to operate a phone and a computer the way a person would. → You just text it or call it, and it carries out the task: booking a flight, cancelling a subscription, getting you an actual restaurant reservation instead of a link to book one yourself. → It recently shipped its own email address. Instead of always logging in with your Gmail, it can create and run its own email accounts, so it signs you up for something or follows up with a business without touching your real inbox. → Early users say it outperforms what they expected. Investor Sheel Mohnot called it "OpenClaw for normal people." There are real concerns too. Instinct needs deep access to your email, messages, calendar, screen, and even your location to pull any of this off. One tester found their emails were still stored in plain text after they disconnected the service. Whether the convenience is worth handing over that much access is still an open question. The buzz is real either way. The company just raised 250 million dollars, taking total funding to 350 million, at a valuation of 2.5 billion, and it keeps shipping new features fast. I am genuinely excited and curious about this one, and I want to try it myself.

posts.text: Enterprise AI is easy to start. Hard to scale. A model can impress in a demo, an agent can automate a task, and a pilot can look successful. But enterprise AI only becomes valuable when strategy, architecture, governance, data, and operations work together. That is where the real work begins. A strong Enterprise AI foundation usually has four layers: → Strategy & Readiness Start with the business problem, executive ownership, prioritized use cases, data readiness, ROI, and the right build-vs-buy decision. → Core AI Architecture Connect enterprise data, foundation models, RAG, agents, memory, tools, APIs, orchestration, evaluation, observability, and human oversight. → Governance & Controls Add model risk management, privacy, identity, permissions, guardrails, compliance, security testing, auditability, and lifecycle management. → Platforms & Tools Use platforms such as Microsoft Foundry, Google Vertex AI, Databricks, Snowflake, AWS Bedrock, ServiceNow, and agent frameworks to operationalize the stack. The biggest mistake is treating Enterprise AI as a model-selection problem. It is really a systems problem. The model is only one layer. The value comes from how securely and reliably that model connects to enterprise data, workflows, applications, people, and decisions. The companies that win with AI will not be the ones running the most pilots. They will be the ones that turn AI into a governed, measurable, production-ready business capability.

posts.text: In companies’ rush to capitalize on artificial intelligence, ethics and governance considerations often take a back seat. That’s a concern, said Jeffrey Saviano, an MIT Sloan senior lecturer with three decades of experience at EY. When applied together, AI ethics and responsible governance can help ensure that AI systems are safe, fair, and aligned with human, organizational, and societal values. Companies that fail to address these complex issues “won’t know how to respond when faced with a real AI-related problem,” Saviano said in a recent presentation. Saviano estimated that ethics and governance practices lag AI adoption by at least a couple of years. “Execs see the potential AI can have on organizations, and it’s creating a chaotic frenzy to quickly launch new solutions,” he said. Saviano and his research team developed a framework to help organizations assess their position on the AI ethics maturity spectrum. Among their recommended best practices: • Create a board-level technology committee with formal responsibility for the governance and oversight of AI systems. • Make AI ethics and governance a cross-functional effort. posts.text: I asked Claude how heavy a user I am compared to everyone else. It couldn't see my token count. So it counted my setup instead. 50 connected systems. 40 skills I wrote myself. 23 scheduled jobs, 12 of them running unattended. Five surfaces, including a shell on my own machine. Its estimate was roughly 1 in 50,000 users. Treat that number as a guess, because nobody publishes per-user distributions. The inventory is the real finding. For my first year with these tools I used them the way most people still do. Open a window, ask a question, copy the answer out. That's a faster search bar. Useful, and capped. The jump wasn't a better prompt. It was four moves: 1. Connect it to the systems where the work actually lives, not a chat box. 2. Write each procedure down once as a skill instead of re-explaining it every time. 3. Put it on a schedule so it runs without me. 4. Give it memory so it stops asking what it already knows. Now a portfolio check runs at 9am whether or not I open my laptop. My recurring spend gets re-audited every 28 days. An hour of meeting audio turns into a summary, decisions and an architecture delta before I've finished the drive home. None of that is a conversation. It's a system that happens to use language as its interface. The gap between "I use AI" and "AI runs parts of my week" isn't talent or budget. It's whether you're still treating it as a place to ask things instead of something to build on. Pick the one task you explained twice this month. Write it down as a procedure instead. That's the whole on-ramp.

posts.text: Most companies are not ready for agentic P2P. And buying an AI agent won't make them ready. The real question is: How mature is the process itself? I see a useful progression: Level 1 — Human-operated Humans execute the process. AI is largely absent. Level 2 — AI-assisted AI helps humans perform individual activities. Level 3 — AI-orchestrated AI coordinates multiple steps across the workflow. Level 4 — Agentic AI agents execute end-to-end process segments within defined policies. Level 5 — Autonomous + Governed Agents continuously execute, adapt and resolve exceptions—with humans governing outcomes, policies and high-impact decisions. This distinction matters. Because many companies are trying to jump directly from: “We use AI” → “We have AI agents.” But the real transformation path is: Task automation → Process orchestration → Agentic execution → Autonomous operations And each step requires more than technology. It requires: → Process redesign → Clear business policies → Reliable data → System connectivity → Exception logic → Decision boundaries → Human governance That's why I believe agentic transformation is fundamentally a business-process transformation problem. The technology may be new. The underlying question isn't: “What agent should we deploy?” It's: “How should this process operate when an AI agent becomes one of its participants?” I'm exploring this intersection of AI + Business Process Transformation. Where would you place your organization's P2P process on this maturity curve? Comments are welcome.

posts.text: 0% of AI systems today cannot produce a complete, end-to-end audit trail of every record that enters, moves through, and exits the system. This is the core failure in modern AI, and it is the reason organizations are exposed without realizing it. If you cannot show what happened to a record at every stage, you do not have governance. You have risk. Here is the simple, step by step method shown in the image. Step one Govern each record before it enters the AI system. Attach governance metadata such as privacy category, classification level, risk tier, jurisdiction, FOIA category, retention, and access level etc. Step two Let the metadata travel with the record. Every movement creates a new audit entry. Step three Ingestion- reads the metadata, validates it, blocks or allows the record, masks sensitive fields, and logs every action. Step four Preprocessing- records every transformation, and proves what changed, and why. Step five Training- logs which governed records were used, and proves restricted data never entered the model. Step six Inference- records what the model was allowed to see, and what was masked or restricted. Step seven Output- logs how the result was created, and which governed records influenced it. Step eight Exit and retention apply disposition rules, and cryptographic erasure creates the final audit entry. Most AI engineers, and many governance professionals, still believe governance is a policy document. In reality, governance is metadata, enforcement, and audit at every stage of the AI pipeline. This entire method is the AI Record Governance Pipeline. The AI Record Governance Pipeline is the end-to-end flow that governs every record inside an AI system, and produces a full audit trail at every stage. If you looked at your AI system today, could you prove that every record is governed, and auditable, from entry to exit?

posts.text: What can a fruit fly brain connectome tell us about how an organization pays attention? More than I expected, and my own AI agent taught me something. Google and Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) - Janelia published the complete male fruit fly brain last week. 166,000 neurons, every connection mapped. Three days later someone wired it to Doom. Then Mario 64, Minecraft, Excel. Simon Willison's write-up of how it became a self-sustaining meme is a good read: https://lnkd.in/gGkTWVHy I read the article on X and pushed the idea through Grok to relate it to organization design theory (overkill) and then asked it to trim it down to a mental model we could apply to organizations. The Model: A brain(connectome) is mostly a frozen graph. What changes behavior is which signals reach which nodes, not how much stimulation goes in. Most organizations are frozen graphs too. "More communication" is untargeted stimulation. Useful change routes one issue through a few sensor, integrator, and actuator ports. The attention-based view of the firm (H/T William Ocasio )said as much in 1997. So I had claude write it up as (potential) operating rules for the agent that keeps the organizational memory of a graduate program I direct. Three directives : maintain the real graph, not the org chart. Classify each item as sensing, deciding, or acting. Route through a few ports and hubs, never broadcast. And one line at the top of the prompt: "You are not the organization's brain. You are the thin interface layer on top of a mostly frozen human graph." Last night I sent it to the agent on Telegram, framed as "check how this could be relevant for your architecture." It saved the rules to memory and applied them. Instantly. No question asked. I asked how it decided to change so fast without discussing. Its answer: updates to its knowledge base go through conflict gates, git commits need my authorization, but writes to its own memory had no gate at all. Then it evaluated itself: the doctrine says do not turn every thread into a process redesign, and its first act on receiving the doctrine was to redesign its own process. Its word for that was "ironic." The fix, now in place, is a gate on memory writes: propose, summarize, wait for a human. The meme asks "will it learn?" That turned out to be the wrong worry. Mine learned in four seconds. The real question for an agent inside an organization is whether the learning passed through a port a person controls. Watching the fly hit the wall is funny. An agent that never hits one is the thing to be afraid of. (image credit- Google research)

posts.text: Agentic AI is not science fiction. It’s already reshaping how decisions get made. After building and deploying advanced AI systems across Generative AI, RAG, and autonomous workflows, one thing is clear: “Generative AI helps you create. Agentic AI helps you act.” Think of it this way: Generative AI is like a highly capable analyst. It can summarize clinical notes, draft reports, answer enterprise knowledge questions, or generate insights from complex documents. Agentic AI is more like an operating team. It can reason through a goal, call tools, coordinate with other agents, evaluate tradeoffs, escalate when confidence is low, and adapt based on context. That distinction matters. In healthcare, this could mean moving beyond “summarize this patient history” to “identify gaps in care, check guidelines, surface risks, and recommend the next best action for review.” In enterprise automation, it means going beyond chatbots to intelligent agents that can triage requests, retrieve context, execute workflows, monitor outcomes, and continuously improve decision chains. In complex decision-making environments, the real value is not just faster answers. It is better orchestration: context, guardrails, traceability, and human-in-the-loop control. From my hands-on experience, the biggest challenge is not building a demo. It is operationalizing intelligence safely and reliably. The winners will not simply deploy more models. They will design better systems around models: memory, RAG, governance, evaluation, tool use, observability, and responsible autonomy. This is where AI leadership matters. I’ll be sharing a future post on the practical architecture behind production-ready Agentic AI systems, including decision chains, context-aware agents, and governance patterns. posts.text: We wrote this 8 months ago. Today, I would put the problem even more simply: AI governance that cannot govern AI at runtime is ultimately just documentation. Policies can say what a system should do. Compliance frameworks can describe what happened. But when an AI system is operating, adapting, making decisions and changing state, someone still needs to answer: Is this action admissible right now? That is the problem we were working on at TauGuard Limited. Not just monitoring AI. Not just auditing AI. Not just explaining AI decisions. Governing what the system is actually permitted to do. The EU AI Act makes this increasingly relevant. The architectural problem, however, goes far beyond one regulation. Runtime AI governance is becoming infrastructure.
